short_description: SAT Solvers: Exceptions, backtracking, and more CPS

exception NotImplemented

(** Types and Exceptions for the Assignment *)

exception Unsatisfiable_formula

type formula =
  | Variable of string
  | Conjunction of formula * formula
  | Disjunction of formula * formula
  | Negation of formula

module Variable_map = Map.Make (String)
module Variable_set = Set.Make (String)

type truth_assignment = bool Variable_map.t

(** Generic scannerless parser combinator modules *)

module IStream : sig
  type t

  val of_string : string -> t
  val uncons : t -> (char * t) option
  val take_while : (char -> bool) -> t -> string * t
end = struct
  type t = { input : string; len : int; index : int }

  let of_string s = { input = s; len = String.length s; index = 0 }
  let advance t = { t with index = t.index + 1 }

  let uncons (is : t) : (char * t) option =
    if is.len = is.index then None else Some (is.input.[is.index], advance is)

  let take_while (p : char -> bool) (is : t) : string * t =
    let s = is.index (* starting index *) in
    let rec aux i =
      if s + i >= is.len || not (p is.input.[s + i]) then i else aux (i + 1)
    in
    let len = aux 0 in
    (String.sub is.input s len, { is with index = is.index + len })
end

module Parser = struct
  let is_alpha = function 'a' .. 'z' | 'A' .. 'Z' -> true | _ -> false
  let is_digit = function '0' .. '9' -> true | _ -> false
  let is_alphanum c = is_alpha c || is_digit c
  let is_whitespace = function ' ' | '\t' | '\r' | '\n' -> true | _ -> false

  type 'a parser = IStream.t -> 'a option * IStream.t

  let run (p : 'a parser) (inp : string) : 'a option =
    IStream.of_string inp |> p |> fst

  let ( <$> ) (f : 'a -> 'b) (p : 'a parser) : 'b parser =
   fun is0 ->
    match p is0 with
    | Some a, is1 -> (Some (f a), is1)
    | None, is1 -> (None, is1)

  let return (x : 'a) : 'a parser = fun is -> (Some x, is)

  let bind (m : 'a parser) (f : 'a -> 'b parser) : 'b parser =
   fun is0 ->
    match m is0 with Some a, is1 -> f a is1 | None, is1 -> (None, is1)

  let ( >>= ) = bind
  let ( $> ) a f = a >>= fun x -> return (f x)
  let ( *> ) m n = m >>= fun _ -> n

  let ( <* ) (p : 'a parser) (q : 'b parser) : 'a parser =
    p >>= fun r ->
    q >>= fun _ -> return r

  let ( <|> ) (p : 'a parser) (q : 'a parser) : 'a parser =
   fun is -> match p is with None, _is1 -> q is | success -> success

  let eof : unit parser =
   fun is ->
    match IStream.uncons is with None -> (Some (), is) | Some _ -> (None, is)

  let satisfy (p : char -> bool) : char parser =
   fun is ->
    match IStream.uncons is with
    | None -> (None, is)
    | Some (c, rest) -> if p c then (Some c, rest) else (None, is)
  (* don't consume the character! *)

  let exact c = satisfy (fun c' -> c = c')

  let satisfy_many (p : char -> bool) : string parser =
   fun is ->
    let str, rest = IStream.take_while p is in
    (Some str, rest)

  let rec many (p : 'a parser) : 'a list parser = some p <|> return []

  and some (p : 'a parser) : 'a list parser =
    p >>= fun x ->
    many p >>= fun xs -> return (x :: xs)

  (** [lexeme p] runs [p], but backtracks if [p] fails, and otherwise consumes
      all whitespace at the start of the remaining input. *)
  let lexeme (p : 'a parser) : 'a parser =
   fun is ->
    match p is with
    | None, _ -> (None, is)
    | Some a, is0 -> ((fun _ -> a) <$> satisfy_many is_whitespace) is0

  let tok c = lexeme (exact c)

  let identifier : string parser =
    let aux =
      satisfy is_alpha >>= fun init ->
      satisfy_many is_alphanum >>= fun rest -> return (String.make 1 init ^ rest)
    in
    lexeme aux
end

module List = struct
  include List

  let rec split_last hd tl =
    match tl with
    | [] -> ([], hd)
    | x :: xs ->
        let ys, last = split_last x xs in
        (hd :: ys, last)
end

(** Formula parsing *)

module rec Formula_parser : sig
  val formula : formula Parser.parser
end = struct
  open Parser

  (*=
      Original grammar:
      <formula> ::=
        | <formula> `&' <formula>       (* Conjunction, right-associative *)
        | <formula> `|' <formula>       (* Disjunction, left-associative  *)
        | `~' <formula>                 (* Negation, right-associative    *)
        | <identifier>                  (* Variable                       *)
        | `(' <formula> `)'             (* Parenthesized                  *)

      Rewritten grammar to handle operator precedence using recursive descent
      and to eliminate left-recursions:

      <formula> ::=
        | <formula1>

      <formula1> ::=
        | <formula2> (`|' <formula2>)*

      <formula2> ::=
        | <formula3> (`&' <formula3>)*

      <formula3> ::=
        | (`~')* <formula4>
      
      <formula4> ::=
        | <identifier>
        | `(' <formula> `)'
  *)
  let formula4 =
    let variable = identifier $> fun v -> Variable v
    and parenthesized = tok '(' *> Formula_parser.formula <* tok ')' in
    parenthesized <|> variable

  let formula3 =
    many (tok '~') >>= fun negations ->
    formula4 $> fun formula ->
    List.fold_right
      (fun _ accumulator -> Negation accumulator)
      negations formula

  let formula2 =
    formula3 >>= fun x ->
    many (tok '&' *> formula3) $> fun xs ->
    let ys, y = List.split_last x xs in
    List.fold_right
      (fun formula accumulator -> Conjunction (formula, accumulator))
      ys y

  let formula1 =
    formula2 >>= fun x ->
    many (tok '|' *> formula2) $> fun xs ->
    List.fold_left
      (fun accumulator formula -> Disjunction (accumulator, formula))
      x xs

  let formula = formula1
end

exception Formula_parsing_error

let parse_formula (input : string) : formula =
  let open Parser in
  match Parser.run (Formula_parser.formula <* eof) input with
  | None -> raise Formula_parsing_error
  | Some formula -> formula

exception Unassigned_variable of string

descr:
In this assignment, we will delve deeper into exception-based backtracking and success/failure continuations, building upon the concepts we've explored in class. You will be tasked with implementing an SAT solver in two ways: exception-based backtracking and CPS.

Introduction: SAT

What is SAT?

In this assignment, you will solve a well-known problem called SAT. SAT is short for "boolean satisfiability." Simply put, if you have a boolean formula with variables, SAT asks if there is any way to assign true and false to each variable so that the value of the formula is true. In this assignment, we write & for boolean AND, | for boolean OR, and ~ for boolean NOT.

For example, the formula x & ~y is satisfiable by assigning x to true and y to false. The formula x & ~x is not satisfiable because no matter what value we give to x, x & ~x will be false.

To represent a boolean formula, we have described it in the prelude as:

type formula =
  | Variable of string
  | Conjunction of formula * formula
  | Disjunction of formula * formula
  | Negation of formula

The Prelude

The prelude for this assignment is much larger than previous assignments. This is because we have given you a parser to help you write tests; see below. For this assignment, you do not need to understand any of the code in the prelude below the definition of the truth_assignment type - but by the end of the course, we hope you will!

Truth Assignments: Variable_map

In order to represent truth assignments, we have defined the Variable_map module for you in the prelude. The module is defined using OCaml's standard Map.Make functor. Read more about it here: Map.

We use Variable_map to define truth assignments: type truth_assignment = bool Variable_map.t.

For example, here is a truth assignment where x is true, and y and z are false:

let xyz_truth_asgn : truth_assignment
    =  Variable_map.empty
    |> Variable_map.add       "x" true
    |> Variable_map.add       "y" false
    |> Variable_map.add       "z" false

Important things to note:

  • Variable_map is not a map itself; it is a module. We will talk about modules more in class the week of the 12th.
  • Variable_map.add does not "mutate" an existing map. It creates a new map with the new key-value pair added. The input map is unchanged and you can still use it!
  • For this assignment, you only need to use the functions Variable_map.empty and Variable_map.add from the Variable_map module.

Writing tests

To write tests, we recommend you create constant truth assignments like the one above, xyz_truth_asgn. Use the function parse_formula : string -> formula in the prelude to produce formulas easily.

For instance, a test case could be (parse_formula "x & ~y | z", xyz_truth_asgn).

Helper functions

We have also provided hidden implementations of the following functions:

  • collect_variables : formula -> string list takes a formula and returns the list of variables that appear in the formula. For example, x & y would return the formula ["x"; "y"].
  • eval : truth_assignment -> formula -> bool takes a truth assignment and a formula and returns whether the formula is true given the assignment.

NOTE: You should use collect_variables and eval in your solutions.

Question 1: Exception-based backtracking

Implement the function find_sat_assignment_exc : formula -> truth_assignment using exception-based backtracking.

This function takes a formula and produces a truth_assignment which makes the formula evaluate to true.

  • If no such assignment exists, you must raise an Unsatisfiable_formula exception.
  • The truth assignment you return must be sharp, which means it must have an assignment for every variable in the expression and no others.
  • If there are multiple truth assignments that make the formula true, return any one of them.

The test cases you must implement for this problem use truth_assignment option as output type. A None output corresponds to find_sat_assignment_exc raising an exception on an unsatisfiable formula given as input. A Some assignment output corresponds to find_sat_assignment_exc returning assignment as a satisfying truth assignment.

Question 2: CPS

Implement the function find_sat_assignment_cps using CPS to find a satisfying assignment to a given formula.

The function takes in the following arguments:

  • formula : formula is the formula we are trying to find a satisfying assignment for
  • return : truth_assignment -> 'r is the success continuation
  • fail : unit -> 'r is the failure continuation

As in Question 1, the assignment you return must be sharp, and if more than one assignment satisfies the formula, you may return any one of them.

NOTE: We will use the tail-call checker on your code again, but to simplify your task and reduce the number of hidden functions that you have to understand, the following functions are allowed to be used in non-tail positions: Variable_map.add, eval, and collect_variables, just like how operators were permitted in the previous assignment.

You do not have to create new tests for this question. We will use the same tests as for question 1. You can think about the tests as calling find_sat_assignment_cps formula (fun x -> Some x) (fun () -> None).

Hints

  • For both questions, you will want to use a recursive inner helper function which does the actual backtracking work.
  • Consider what you should be backtracking over: it doesn't make any sense to be searching through the formula!
  • There should be a more-than-passing similarity between your two solutions. Take special note of this: a future exam will almost certainly ask you to translate from one of the three types of backtracking to another.
  • There is a lot of grading code for this assignment to help you understand the inputs and expected outputs for each test case. As a result, the grader is a bit slower than usual. Expect to see the "Grader is taking a lot of time" message for a few seconds. If it goes for longer than a few seconds, the issue is in your code.
